## Why This Matters

Real records are often **ragged**. Picture a course catalog: some courses list prerequisites, some
charge a lab fee, some do neither, and each nests a schedule. You have two honest ways to manage data
like this -- force it into a fixed **relational table** and ask questions in **SQL**, or keep each
record's own shape in a **document store** and query the shapes directly. Each way buys something and
costs something. The working skill is not picking a side; it is recognizing which shape your data
wants -- and most real teams run both.

::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy: the warehouse and the order form"}
A relational database is a well-organized warehouse, and SQL is the order form. You do not wander the
aisles looping over rows -- you hand in a form describing *what* you want, and the query engine works
out the fastest way to fetch it. That declarative style is why the same query runs unchanged on a
laptop or a cluster.
:::

## The Relational Way: Tables and SQL

A **relational table** is rows (records) by columns (fields), each column named and typed -- a
spreadsheet with rules. You retrieve from it with `SELECT`:

```sql
SELECT department, AVG(credits) AS avg_credits   -- which columns (and computed values)
FROM courses                                     -- which table
WHERE lab_fee IS NOT NULL                         -- keep only some rows
GROUP BY department                               -- one output row per department
ORDER BY avg_credits DESC;                         -- sort the result
```

Read it in **execution order**, not written order: `FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> SELECT -> ORDER BY`.
You describe the *result you want*; the engine decides *how* to compute it. This is the same
group-and-aggregate shape you have already met twice -- the pandas `groupby` from L02 and the Spark
`groupBy` from L04 -- now in its original, declarative form.

When data is split across **two** tables, a **join** stitches them back together on a shared key --
for example, courses and the departments that own them:

```sql
SELECT c.code, d.dept_name           -- read-only illustration (the lab uses one table)
FROM courses c
JOIN departments d ON c.department = d.dept_id;
```

A join is how the relational model keeps each fact in one place and recombines facts on demand.

## OLTP vs OLAP: Two Jobs, Two Layouts

Not all databases do the same job:

| | **OLTP** (transactional) | **OLAP** (analytical) |
|---|---|---|
| Job | run the business: insert/update one row at a time | understand the business: scan many rows, few columns |
| Example | "record this enrollment" | "average credits by department" |
| Engine | PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite | **DuckDB**, BigQuery, Snowflake |
| Storage | **row**-oriented | **column**-oriented |

Analysis is OLAP work, and this is exactly L03's storage story: to average one column over many rows,
a **column store reads only that column** (and compresses it well, because neighbors are alike),
while a row store must touch every row. You measured that gap on CSV vs Parquet in L03; columnar SQL
engines win analytical queries for the same reason.

**DuckDB** is an in-process OLAP database -- "SQLite for analytics." There is no server to install
(`pip install duckdb`), and it queries data files and pandas DataFrames directly, with real SQL and
columnar speed. It is the lab's SQL engine.

## The Document Way: Schema-on-Write vs Schema-on-Read

The deepest difference between relational and NoSQL is *when structure is enforced*:

| | Schema-on-write (relational) | Schema-on-read (NoSQL) |
|---|---|---|
| Structure checked | when data is **stored** -- a wrong shape is rejected | when data is **used** -- your code handles whatever arrives |
| Ragged data (optional fields, lists) | NULL-padded columns, awkward | natural -- each document keeps its own shape |
| Guarantee to later readers | strong: every row has every column, typed | weak: each document may differ |
| Schema changes | migrate the table | just start writing the new shape |

Neither is "better" -- they move the same work (handling shape) to different places. To put ragged
records into a table you must **flatten** them (pandas `json_normalize` does this): optional fields
become NULL-padded columns, and nested lists end up stranded inside single cells. A document store
skips that step and stores each record as-is.

::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy: apartments and self-storage"}
A relational table is an apartment building: every unit has the same floor plan, so the address
system is simple and the building scales cleanly. A document store is a self-storage facility: each
unit holds whatever shape you bring, labeled by a key -- at the price of nobody guaranteeing what is
inside any given unit.
:::

## The NoSQL Families

"NoSQL" is an umbrella, not one design. The families you should be able to place:

| Family | Unit of storage | Canonical tools | Typical use |
|--------|-----------------|-----------------|-------------|
| **Document** | a JSON-like document, queried by content | MongoDB; **TinyDB** (the lab's zero-server stand-in) | ragged records: catalogs, profiles, saved payloads |
| **Key-value** | an opaque value behind a key | Redis | caches, sessions: "give me exactly this one thing, fast" |
| **Wide-column** | sparse rows with per-row columns, spread across machines | Cassandra | huge write-heavy tables: sensor feeds, message stores |
| **Graph** | nodes and edges | Neo4j | relationship-first questions -- the subject of Unit VII |

Document stores are this lesson's focus. Cassandra and Redis are named so you can place them on the
map; they are servers, so we use **TinyDB** -- a tiny, file-based document store -- to feel the
document model without running infrastructure.

## Which to Choose When

- **Relational (SQL)** when: the data is genuinely tabular, many tools or people will query it,
  aggregations dominate, or you need the schema as a *contract* for later readers.
- **Document (NoSQL)** when: records are ragged or deeply nested, the shape evolves often, or you
  mostly fetch whole records by content.
- **Mixed is normal:** a common pipeline lands raw, ragged data in a document store, then flattens
  the analysis-ready slice into tables -- each store where it is strong.

::: {.callout-warning}
NoSQL is not a SQL upgrade. Skipping schema design does not remove the work -- it moves it into every
program that reads the data, forever. Choose schema-on-read because the *data* is ragged, not because
schema design feels like effort.
:::

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"If I know pandas, why learn SQL?"** -- Because the data usually arrives *in* a database, and
pushing the filter and aggregation to the engine (instead of loading everything into Python) is
faster, uses less memory, and is what every data team does. SQL is also far more portable across jobs
and tools than any one library's API.

**"Is SQL dying, then?"** -- The opposite: it keeps absorbing its challengers. Document databases grew
SQL-like query layers, and engines like DuckDB read JSON directly. The professional skill is not
picking a side; it is recognizing which shape your data wants -- most teams run both.
